Snobby describes a person who believes they are better than others — and who actually shows this belief through the way they talk, act, or treat people. A snobby person doesn't just quietly feel superior; they make others feel inferior, often without saying it directly.
What a Snobby Person Actually Does

A snobby person:

  • Looks down on others who they think are less wealthy, less educated, less stylish, or less cultured than themselves.
  • Acts cold, dismissive, or uninterested toward people they consider "below" them. They might not greet someone, give short replies, or simply ignore them.
  • Is easily impressed by status — things like expensive brands, prestigious schools, famous names, or high social positions. They quickly warm up to people with status and quickly cool down toward those without it.
  • Judges people for their choices in ways that feel unkind — for example, quietly mocking someone for the food they eat, the music they like, the clothes they wear, or the place they grew up.
  • Talks about themselves or their world in a way that excludes others — name-dropping expensive restaurants, mentioning elite schools, or referencing experiences that only wealthy or privileged people would have, as if everyone should relate to this.
The Key Feeling Behind "Snobby"

The heart of "snobby" is a mix of two things happening at once:

  1. A feeling of personal superiority — "I am better, more refined, more sophisticated than you."
  2. A display of that feeling — acting in a way that makes others feel small, unwelcome, or judged.

A person can be snobby without saying a single rude word. A glance, a raised eyebrow, a cold silence, or a subtle smirk can all be snobby. It's about an attitude that comes through, not just spoken words.
Different Areas Where Someone Can Be Snobby

Snobbiness is not limited to wealth or social class. A person can be snobby about almost anything they feel superior in:

  • Social class / money: Looks down on people who are less wealthy or from a "lower" background. Might refuse to socialize with someone because they don't live in the "right" neighborhood or went to the "wrong" school.
  • Education / intelligence: Treats people as lesser for not having a university degree, or for not knowing about philosophy, literature, or science. Might correct others in a condescending way.
  • Food / drink: Dismisses people who eat simple or popular food. ("You drink instant coffee? I only drink single-origin, hand-roasted beans.")
  • Art, music, or film: Looks down on people who enjoy popular movies, pop music, or mainstream entertainment. ("You liked that film? It was so shallow.")
  • Fashion / brands: Judges people based on whether their clothes or accessories are expensive or designer.
  • Accent or dialect: Acts as though a certain way of speaking is "proper" and others are inferior.

The subject changes, but the attitude is always the same: "I have refined taste / superior knowledge / better background — and you don't."
The Crucial Difference: Snobby vs. Simply Having Preferences

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise.

Having preferences or high standards is NOT the same as being snobby.

  • A person who personally prefers classical music but enjoys talking to someone who loves pop music → not snobby.
  • A person who prefers classical music and makes the pop music fan feel stupid or uncultured for their taste → snobby.

The difference is not what you like. It's whether you use your preferences as a weapon to rank people. A snobby person doesn't just prefer things — they use those preferences to build a wall between themselves and people they consider inferior.

You can have the most sophisticated taste in the world and be completely warm, humble, and welcoming. That is not snobby. Snobbery begins the moment you start treating others as lesser beings because of what they like, where they come from, or what they have.
What It Feels Like to Be on the Receiving End

When a person is snobby toward you, you typically feel:

  • Looked down upon or judged — as if you said or did something wrong just by being yourself.
  • Unwelcome or excluded — as if you don't belong in their company.
  • Self-conscious or small — questioning your own choices, background, or worth.
  • Dismissed — as if your presence or opinion doesn't really matter to them.

This is why "snobby" is a negative word. It's not simply describing someone with high standards. It's describing someone whose behavior makes others feel inferior, disrespected, or invisible.
Degree and Intensity

"Snobby" can apply to mild or strong versions of this behavior:

  • Mildly snobby: Someone who is a little bit aloof about their taste in wine and gently wrinkles their nose at cheap brands, but doesn't go out of their way to make others feel bad.
  • Very snobby: Someone who openly mocks others' choices, refuses to engage with people they consider beneath them, and constantly signals their own superiority.

The word "snobby" covers the whole range, though it always implies a negative judgment of the person being described.
How It's Used in Sentences

• "She was so snobby at the party — she wouldn't even talk to anyone who didn't go to a private school."
  • "Don't be snobby about food. Not everyone can afford to eat at fancy restaurants."
  • "He's a bit snobby about books. If you haven't read the classics, he acts like you're not worth his time."
  • "I expected the staff at that boutique to be snobby, but they were actually very friendly."
  • "Growing up wealthy made her snobby without her even realizing it."
Related Words (Same Family)

• Snob (noun) — the person who behaves this way. "He's such a snob."
  • Snobbishly (adverb) — describes how someone does something with this attitude. "She snobbishly refused to sit at our table."
  • Snobbery / snobbishness (noun) — the quality or behavior itself. "His snobbery made him very unpopular."
  • Snobbish (adjective) — a slightly more formal version of snobby, meaning exactly the same thing.
Words That Mean the Opposite

To fully understand "snobby," it helps to know its opposites:

  • Down-to-earth — treats everyone as an equal, regardless of background or status.
  • Humble — doesn't think of themselves as better than others.
  • Unpretentious — doesn't try to seem more sophisticated or important than they are.
  • Warm or welcoming — makes people feel included and valued.
A One-Line Summary

If you had to boil it down to one sentence:

A snobby person acts superior to others and makes those they consider "beneath" them feel judged, unwelcome, or small — based on things like money, taste, education, or social class.
